about: CEGE0101 is a 15-credit Term 1 module in UCL's Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering that introduces structural engineering: how simple determinate structures such as pin-jointed trusses, beams and frames behave under load, and the basic tools to analyse them. Its learning outcomes run from Newton's laws and free body diagrams through truss analysis, shear force and bending moment diagrams, beam stresses and deflections and virtual work, to elastic buckling. According to the 2026/27 UCL module catalogue it is assessed by an exam (70%) and two group activities (30%).

notes.h: Newton's laws, equilibrium and free body diagrams
notes.body:
Everything in this module rests on one idea: a structure that is not accelerating is in equilibrium, so the forces and moments acting on it (or on any part of it) must balance.

Newton's laws in structural terms:
- First law: a body stays at rest (or moves at constant velocity) unless a resultant force acts. A building or bridge at rest therefore has zero resultant force and zero resultant moment.
- Second law: F = ma. In statics a = 0, so ΣF = 0.
- Third law: action and reaction are equal and opposite. When you cut a structure, the internal force on one side of the cut is equal and opposite to the force on the other side. This is what lets us split a structure into free bodies.

Equilibrium in two dimensions gives three independent equations:
- ΣFx = 0 (horizontal forces)
- ΣFy = 0 (vertical forces)
- ΣM = 0 about any point (choose a point that eliminates unknowns)

Supports and the reactions they provide:
- Roller: one reaction, perpendicular to the surface.
- Pin: two reaction components (horizontal and vertical), no moment.
- Fixed (encastré): two force components plus a moment.

The free body diagram (FBD) is the most important habit you can build. Draw the body isolated from its surroundings; replace every support by its reactions; show all applied loads with values and positions; mark dimensions; and choose a sign convention (for example, up and right positive, anticlockwise moments positive). Unknown reactions can be drawn in any direction: a negative answer simply means the real force acts the other way.

Worked example: a simply supported beam AB of span 6 m (pin at A, roller at B) carries a 30 kN point load 2 m from A.
- Moments about A: R_B × 6 − 30 × 2 = 0, so R_B = 10 kN.
- Vertical equilibrium: R_A + R_B = 30, so R_A = 20 kN.
- Horizontal: no horizontal loads, so the horizontal reaction at A is zero.
Check: moments about B give R_A × 6 = 30 × 4, so R_A = 20 kN. The support nearer the load takes more of it.

Distributed loads: replace a uniformly distributed load (UDL) w (kN/m) over length a by a single resultant wa acting at the middle of that length, but only for finding reactions. For internal forces you must cut the beam first and then take the resultant of the part of the load on the free body.

Exam tips: always draw the FBD before writing equations, take moments about the point with most unknowns, and use the unused equation as a check.

A structure is statically determinate if all its reactions and internal forces can be found from equilibrium alone. If there are more unknowns than independent equilibrium equations, it is statically indeterminate (hyperstatic), and you also need compatibility (how members deform) and the material law. If there are too few restraints or members, it is a mechanism and cannot carry general loads.

Why it matters:
- Determinate structures are easy to analyse by hand and are not stressed by support settlement, temperature change or lack of fit, because they can adjust freely.
- Indeterminate structures have alternative load paths (redundancy) and usually smaller moments and deflections, but they need more advanced methods and attract stresses from settlement and temperature.

Counting checks in 2D (r = number of reaction components):

Beams: compare r with 3 (plus one extra equation for each internal pin, c).
- Simply supported (pin + roller): r = 3, determinate.
- Propped cantilever (fixed + roller): r = 4, one degree indeterminate.
- Continuous beam over three supports (pin + two rollers): r = 4, one degree indeterminate.

Pin-jointed trusses (m members, j joints): degree of indeterminacy = m + r − 2j.
- Triangle on pin and roller: 3 + 3 − 6 = 0, determinate.
- Square panel with one diagonal: 5 + 3 − 8 = 0, determinate.
- Square panel with both diagonals: 6 + 3 − 8 = 1, one redundant member.
- Square panel with no diagonal: 4 + 3 − 8 = −1, a mechanism.

Rigid-jointed plane frames: degree = 3m + r − 3j − c, where c is the number of releases (for example, an internal pin in a frame adds one condition, M = 0).
- Portal frame (3 members, 4 joints) with fixed bases: 9 + 6 − 12 = 3.
- Same frame with pinned bases: 9 + 4 − 12 = 1.
- Three-pinned portal (pinned bases plus a pin at the crown): 9 + 4 − 12 − 1 = 0, determinate.

Important caution: the count is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. A structure can satisfy the count and still be geometrically unstable, for example if all reactions are parallel (three rollers on a flat surface) or all pass through one point, or if one part of a truss has too many members while another part has too few. Always look at the geometry as well as the numbers.

External versus internal indeterminacy: a truss can be externally determinate (three reaction components) but internally redundant (an extra diagonal), or the other way round.

Exam tips: state the formula, define every symbol, show the count, then comment on stability; examiners reward the comment as much as the arithmetic.

notes.h: Linear elastic behaviour and structural members
notes.body:
Most first-year structural analysis assumes linear elastic material behaviour: deformation is proportional to load, and the structure returns to its original shape when the load is removed.

Key definitions:
- Direct stress σ = F/A (N/mm², which is the same as MPa). Tension is usually taken as positive.
- Direct strain ε = ΔL/L (dimensionless).
- Hooke's law: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus. Typical approximate values: structural steel about 200–210 GPa, concrete about 30 GPa (varies with strength), structural timber roughly 7–14 GPa along the grain.
- Axial extension of a uniform bar: δ = FL/(EA). The product EA is the axial stiffness of the section; EA/L is the stiffness of the bar.
- Poisson's ratio ν: the ratio of lateral contraction to axial strain (about 0.3 for steel).
- Thermal strain: ε = αΔT; a free bar expands without stress, a fully restrained bar develops stress EαΔT.

Worked example: a steel tie of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 500 mm² carries 50 kN, with E = 200 GPa = 200 000 N/mm².
- σ = 50 000/500 = 100 N/mm².
- ε = 100/200 000 = 5 × 10⁻⁴.
- δ = εL = 5 × 10⁻⁴ × 2000 = 1.0 mm.
Keep units consistent: N, mm and N/mm² is the safest set.

The stress–strain curve of mild steel: a linear region up to the yield stress, a yield plateau, strain hardening and finally necking and fracture. Ductile materials (steel) give warning before failure; brittle materials (cast iron, unreinforced concrete in tension) do not. Linear elastic analysis is valid while stresses stay below yield.

Superposition: because response is linear, the effects of several loads can be added. This only holds while the material is elastic and deflections are small enough that geometry does not change significantly.

Types of structural member and what they carry:
- Ties: axial tension only (cables, hangers, truss tension members).
- Struts and columns: axial compression; slender ones can fail by buckling.
- Beams: transverse loads carried by bending and shear.
- Members of rigid frames: combinations of axial force, shear and bending.
- Cables and arches: funicular forms that carry load in pure tension (cables) or mainly compression (arches).

Engineers place these members in the wider design context: loads flow from slabs to beams, to columns, to foundations and finally to the ground. Following this load path is the first step in any analysis.

Exam tips: show units at every line, quote E with its units, and say explicitly that the answer assumes linear elasticity (stress below yield).

A pin-jointed truss is idealised as straight members connected by frictionless pins, with loads applied only at the joints. Each member is therefore a two-force member carrying only axial tension or compression; there is no bending.

Sign convention: tension positive (member pulls on the joint), compression negative (member pushes on the joint). Draw every unknown member force as tension pulling away from the joint; a negative result then means compression.

Method of joints:
- Find the reactions from the whole-structure FBD.
- Start at a joint with no more than two unknown forces.
- Use ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at that joint (moments are automatically satisfied at a pin).
- Move from joint to joint.

Worked example: a triangular truss with span AB = 4 m and apex C at mid-span, 1.5 m high, carries 30 kN downwards at C. A is pinned, B is a roller.
- By symmetry, R_A = R_B = 15 kN upwards.
- Rafter length = √(2² + 1.5²) = 2.5 m, so sin θ = 0.6 and cos θ = 0.8.
- Joint A, vertical: 15 + F_AC × 0.6 = 0, so F_AC = −25 kN (25 kN compression).
- Joint A, horizontal: F_AB + F_AC × 0.8 = 0, so F_AB = +20 kN (20 kN tension).
The rafters push, and the bottom tie stops the supports spreading.

Method of sections: cut through no more than three members whose lines of action do not all meet at one point, and take moments about the point where two of the cut members intersect. This gives one member force directly.

Example: a Pratt truss of four 3 m panels and height 4 m carries 20 kN at each of the three interior bottom joints (reactions 30 kN each). Cut the second panel:
- Top chord: moments about the bottom joint at 6 m: 30 × 6 − 20 × 3 = 120 kN·m, so the force is 120/4 = 30 kN compression.
- Bottom chord: moments about the top joint at 3 m: 30 × 3 = 90 kN·m, so the force is 90/4 = 22.5 kN tension.
- Diagonal (3–4–5 geometry, sloping down towards mid-span): it must carry the panel shear 30 − 20 = 10 kN vertically, so its force is 10 × 5/4 = 12.5 kN tension.
Check horizontally: −30 + 22.5 + 0.6 × 12.5 = 0.

Zero-force members (useful shortcuts):
- At an unloaded joint with two non-collinear members, both are zero-force.
- At an unloaded joint where two members are collinear, the third member is zero-force.
Zero-force members are not useless: they brace compression members and carry load under other load cases.

Exam tips: state the convention, draw arrows for tension away from joints, and always do a final check equation.

notes.h: Shear force and bending moment diagrams for beams
notes.body:
Internal forces in a beam are found by cutting it at a section and applying equilibrium to the part on one side.

Sign convention used here (state yours in any answer):
- Shear force V at a section: the sum of the vertical forces to the left of the section, positive when that sum acts upwards.
- Bending moment M: positive when sagging (beam bends concave upwards, bottom fibre in tension), negative when hogging.

Relationships (with w the downward load intensity):
- dV/dx = −w: the slope of the SFD equals minus the load intensity.
- dM/dx = V: the slope of the BMD equals the shear force.
- So the maximum bending moment occurs where V = 0 (or changes sign).
- A point load causes a jump in the SFD; a concentrated moment causes a jump in the BMD.
- Unloaded lengths: V constant, M linear. UDL: V linear, M parabolic.

Standard results for a simply supported span L:
- Central point load P: reactions P/2, M_max = PL/4 at mid-span.
- UDL w: reactions wL/2, M_max = wL²/8 at mid-span. For L = 8 m and w = 10 kN/m: reactions 40 kN, M_max = 80 kN·m.
- Point load P at distance a from A and b from B: M_max = Pab/L under the load.

Cantilever of length L, fixed at one end:
- Tip load P: hogging moment PL at the support.
- UDL w: hogging moment wL²/2 at the support.

Worked example (overhang): beam with a pin at A (x = 0), a roller at B (x = 6 m) and an overhang to C (x = 8 m), carrying 10 kN/m along its whole 8 m length.
- Total load 80 kN acting at x = 4 m. Moments about A: R_B × 6 = 80 × 4, so R_B = 53.3 kN and R_A = 26.7 kN.
- In the span, V = 26.7 − 10x, which is zero at x = 2.67 m. M there = 26.7 × 2.67 − 5 × 2.67² = 35.6 kN·m (sagging).
- At B, the overhang gives M = −10 × 2²/2 = −20 kN·m (hogging).
- In the span, M = 26.7x − 5x² = 0 at x = 5.33 m. This is the point of contraflexure, where the moment changes sign.

Procedure for drawing: find reactions; mark key points (supports, point loads, ends of UDLs); compute V and M at each; join with the correct shapes (straight or parabolic); label the maximum values and their positions.

Exam tips: draw the SFD directly under the loaded beam and the BMD under that, line up key points vertically, and label values with units. Points of contraflexure matter in practice because reinforced concrete needs steel on the tension face, which switches sides there.

notes.h: Shear and bending stresses in beams
notes.body:
Simple (Euler–Bernoulli) bending theory assumes plane sections remain plane, the material is linear elastic with the same E in tension and compression, and the beam bends about a principal axis. It gives the engineer's bending equation:

M/I = σ/y = E/R

- M: bending moment at the section.
- I: second moment of area about the neutral axis.
- y: distance from the neutral axis (which passes through the centroid in elastic bending).
- σ: bending stress at distance y; R: radius of curvature.

Stress varies linearly with y: zero at the neutral axis and largest at the extreme fibres. Maximum stress σ_max = M/Z, where Z = I/y_max is the elastic section modulus.

Rectangle b wide and d deep: I = bd³/12 and Z = bd²/6. Depth is far more effective than width, which is why beams are deep and narrow and why I-sections put material in the flanges.

Worked example: a timber beam 100 mm wide and 300 mm deep carries M = 20 kN·m = 20 × 10⁶ N·mm.
- Z = 100 × 300²/6 = 1.5 × 10⁶ mm³.
- σ_max = 20 × 10⁶/1.5 × 10⁶ = 13.3 N/mm² (compression at the top and tension at the bottom for sagging).
- If the same beam were laid on its side (b = 300, d = 100), Z = 0.5 × 10⁶ mm³ and the stress would be three times larger, 40 N/mm².

Non-symmetric sections (for example a T-section): find the centroid first, then use the parallel axis theorem I = Σ(I_own + A h²), where h is the distance from each part's centroid to the section centroid. For a T with a 200 × 20 mm flange on a 20 × 180 mm web, the centroid is 57.4 mm below the top and I ≈ 28.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The extreme fibre distances differ (57.4 mm and 142.6 mm), so the stresses at top and bottom differ.

Shear stress: τ = VQ/(Ib), where V is the shear force, Q = Aȳ is the first moment of the area beyond the level considered (about the neutral axis), and b is the width at that level.
- In a rectangle the distribution is parabolic: zero at the top and bottom, maximum at the neutral axis, τ_max = 1.5V/A.
- Example: V = 30 kN on the 100 × 300 mm section: τ_max = 1.5 × 30 000/30 000 = 1.5 N/mm².
- In an I-section the web carries nearly all the shear, and τ in the web is close to V/(web area).

In ordinary beams, bending stress usually governs over shear stress; shear matters near supports, under large point loads, in short deep beams and in timber (which is weak in longitudinal shear).

Exam tips: convert kN·m to N·mm (multiply by 10⁶), state which fibre is in tension, and sketch the stress distributions as well as quoting the numbers.

Beams must be stiff enough as well as strong enough: excessive deflection cracks finishes, causes ponding and makes floors feel bouncy. Deflection is a serviceability check.

Governing equation (small deflections, linear elastic, Euler–Bernoulli bending):

EI d²v/dx² = M(x)

with v the deflection (positive upwards) and M positive when sagging. EI is the flexural rigidity.

Double integration method:
- Write M(x) for each region of the beam.
- Integrate once to get the slope EI dv/dx = ∫M dx + C₁.
- Integrate again for EI v = ∫∫M dx dx + C₁x + C₂.
- Find the constants from boundary conditions: v = 0 at a pin or roller; v = 0 and dv/dx = 0 at a fixed support.
- Macaulay's (singularity function) notation lets one expression cover a beam with several point loads.

Derivation for a cantilever of length L, fixed at x = 0, with a tip load P downwards:
- M(x) = −P(L − x) (hogging).
- EI v′ = −P(Lx − x²/2) + C₁, and v′(0) = 0 gives C₁ = 0.
- EI v = −P(Lx²/2 − x³/6) + C₂, and v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = 0.
- At the tip: v = −PL³/(3EI), so the tip deflects PL³/(3EI) downwards.

Standard results worth memorising:
- Cantilever, tip load P: δ = PL³/(3EI); tip slope PL²/(2EI).
- Cantilever, UDL w: δ = wL⁴/(8EI).
- Simply supported, central point load P: δ = PL³/(48EI) at mid-span.
- Simply supported, UDL w: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI) at mid-span.

Worked example: a simply supported steel beam of span 6 m carries 10 kN/m. E = 200 GPa, I = 80 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Work in N and mm (10 kN/m = 10 N/mm).
- δ = 5 × 10 × 6000⁴/(384 × 200 000 × 80 × 10⁶) = 10.5 mm.
- A typical serviceability limit such as span/360 gives 16.7 mm (actual limits depend on the code, the use and the finishes), so this beam would be acceptable on that criterion.

Points to notice:
- Deflection depends on L³ (point loads) or L⁴ (UDL), so span is the dominant variable: doubling the span of a UDL-loaded beam multiplies the deflection by 16.
- Deflection is inversely proportional to E and I, so stiffness is improved by deeper sections (I ∝ d³ for a rectangle).
- Superposition: deflections from separate load cases can be added while the beam stays elastic.

Exam tips: state your sign convention for v and M, write the boundary conditions explicitly, and keep units consistent (N, mm, N/mm²).

notes.h: Virtual work: deflections of trusses and frames
notes.body:
The principle of virtual work gives a powerful, general way to find the deflection at any point of a structure. For a deformable body in equilibrium, the external virtual work equals the internal virtual work. In the unit load method, a virtual unit load is applied at the point and in the direction of the deflection wanted, and the real deformations are used.

Unit load method:
1 × δ = Σ (internal forces from the unit load) × (real deformations of the members)

For a pin-jointed truss (linear elastic members):
δ = Σ F u L/(EA)
- F: member force from the real loads.
- u: member force from a unit load at the point and in the direction of δ.
- L, E, A: length, modulus and area of each member.
- Use the same sign convention (tension positive) for F and u. A positive δ is in the direction of the unit load.

Worked example: the triangular truss with span 4 m, rise 1.5 m and 30 kN at the apex has F = −25 kN in each 2.5 m rafter and +20 kN in the 4 m tie. A unit vertical load at the apex gives u = −25/30 = −0.833 in each rafter and +20/30 = +0.667 in the tie.
- Σ FuL = 2 × (−25)(−0.833)(2.5) + 20 × 0.667 × 4 = 104.2 + 53.3 = 157.5 kN·m.
- With E = 200 GPa and A = 1000 mm², EA = 200 000 kN, so δ = 157.5/200 000 = 7.9 × 10⁻⁴ m ≈ 0.79 mm downwards.
Setting the work out as a table (member, L, F, u, FuL) avoids mistakes.

Lack of fit and temperature: replace FL/(EA) by the actual change in member length (for example αΔT L), so δ = Σ u ΔL.

For beams and frames (bending dominant, axial and shear deformation neglected):
δ = ∫ M m dx/(EI)
- M: bending moment from the real loads; m: bending moment from the unit load.
- Use the same sign convention for M and m in each member.
- Check: for a cantilever with tip load P, M = Px and m = x (x from the tip), so δ = ∫₀ᴸ Px² dx/EI = PL³/(3EI), matching the standard result.
- For rotations, apply a unit moment instead of a unit force.
- Product integrals for common shapes (rectangle × triangle, triangle × triangle) can be read from tables to speed up the integration.

Worked frame example: an L-shaped frame with a vertical column of height h = 3 m fixed at its base and a horizontal arm of length a = 2 m carries P = 10 kN downwards at the free end; EI = 20 000 kN·m² throughout.
- Vertical deflection: arm M = Px, m = x; column M = Pa, m = a. δ_v = (Pa³/3 + Pa²h)/EI = (26.7 + 120)/20 000 = 7.3 mm.
- Horizontal deflection: a unit horizontal load at the tip gives m = 0 in the arm and m = y in the column (y measured down from the top), so δ_h = Pah²/(2EI) = 90/20 000 = 4.5 mm.

Exam tips: tabulate member values, keep units in kN and m (EA in kN, EI in kN·m²), and state the direction of the answer.

notes.h: Shear force and bending moment diagrams for frames
notes.body:
A rigid-jointed frame (such as a portal frame) has members connected by joints that transmit moment. Each member can carry axial force, shear force and bending moment, and the diagrams are drawn along each member.

Drawing conventions:
- Treat each member as a beam with its own local axis; resolve loads into components along and perpendicular to that member.
- In UK civil engineering practice, bending moment diagrams for frames are commonly drawn on the tension side of each member, so no plus or minus sign is needed: the side of the diagram shows which face is in tension. State this convention in your answer.
- Axial force and shear diagrams need an explicit sign convention.

Rules at a rigid joint:
- For a two-member joint with no external moment applied, the moment just inside one member equals the moment just inside the other: the BMD is continuous around the corner, on the same (inside or outside) face.
- At a pin or a free end, M = 0 (unless a concentrated moment is applied there).
- The shear in one member becomes axial force in a perpendicular member at a right-angled joint.

Procedure:
1. Check determinacy (3m + r − 3j − c = 0).
2. Find reactions from overall equilibrium, plus extra equations from internal pins (M = 0 at a pin, applied to the part on one side).
3. Cut each member near its ends, find N, V and M, then plot.

Worked example: three-pinned portal frame. Columns of height h = 5 m with pinned bases, a horizontal beam of span L = 10 m with a pin at mid-span, and a UDL w = 10 kN/m on the beam.
- Vertical reactions by symmetry: wL/2 = 50 kN each.
- Moments about the crown pin for the left half: 50 × 5 − H × 5 − 10 × 5 × 2.5 = 0, so H = 25 kN (general result wL²/(8h)). The bases push inwards on the frame.
- Column: M rises linearly from zero at the base to Hh = 125 kN·m at the knee, tension on the outside face.
- Beam: M(x) = −125 + 50x − 5x², which is zero at the crown (x = 5 m), as it must be at a pin.
Note that the knee moment here equals wL²/8, the simply supported span moment, but with opposite sense.

Sway: an unsymmetrical frame, or a frame under horizontal (wind) load, sways sideways. In a determinate frame the reactions still follow from statics, but the diagrams are no longer symmetrical.

The L-shaped cantilever frame (fixed base, horizontal arm, tip load P) is a good first example: the arm BMD is triangular (zero at the tip, Pa at the corner), and the column carries a constant moment Pa plus an axial compression P.

Exam tips: draw the frame FBD with all reaction components, show values at every joint and mid-span, and check that moments balance at each rigid joint.

A slender member in compression can fail by buckling (a sudden sideways instability) at a load well below the load that would crush it. Euler's theory gives the elastic critical load for an ideal column.

Assumptions of the Euler model:
- Initially perfectly straight, with the load applied exactly along the centroidal axis.
- Linear elastic, homogeneous material.
- Small deflections; buckling about the axis with the smaller I.

Euler critical load for a pin-ended column:
P_cr = π²EI/L²

Derivation outline: in a slightly bent position, M = −Pv, so EI v″ + Pv = 0. The solution v = A sin(kx) + B cos(kx), with k² = P/(EI), must satisfy v = 0 at both ends, so kL = nπ. The lowest non-zero load (n = 1) is π²EI/L².

Other end conditions, using an effective length L_e = kL:
- Pinned–pinned: L_e = L.
- Fixed–free (flagpole): L_e = 2L, so P_cr is a quarter of the pinned value.
- Fixed–pinned: L_e ≈ 0.7L.
- Fixed–fixed: L_e = 0.5L, so P_cr is four times the pinned value.
Then P_cr = π²EI/L_e². (Design codes use somewhat different effective lengths to allow for imperfect fixity.)

Slenderness:
- Radius of gyration r = √(I/A).
- Slenderness ratio λ = L_e/r.
- Critical stress σ_cr = P_cr/A = π²E/λ².
Euler theory only applies where σ_cr is below the yield stress, that is for slender members. Short, stocky columns fail by squashing (P = f_y A) instead.

Worked example: a solid steel bar, diameter 50 mm, length 3 m, pinned at both ends; E = 200 GPa, f_y = 275 N/mm².
- I = πd⁴/64 = 3.07 × 10⁵ mm⁴; A = 1963 mm².
- P_cr = π² × 200 000 × 3.07 × 10⁵/3000² = 67.3 kN.
- Squash load = 275 × 1963 = 540 kN, so buckling governs by a wide margin.
- r = d/4 = 12.5 mm, λ = 3000/12.5 = 240, σ_cr = 34 N/mm² (well below yield, so Euler applies).
- As a fixed–free cantilever column of the same length, P_cr would be 67.3/4 = 16.8 kN.

Real columns: initial crookedness, eccentric loading and residual stresses mean real columns fail below both the Euler load and the squash load, especially at intermediate slenderness. Design codes (for example Eurocode 3 for steel) use buckling curves based on this interaction; first-year work focuses on understanding the Euler result and its limits.

Ways to increase buckling resistance: reduce the effective length (bracing, fixity), increase I (spread material away from the axis, as in hollow sections), or use a stiffer material.

Exam tips: always check which axis has the smaller I, state the end conditions and effective length, and compare the Euler load with the squash load.

cards.f: Three equilibrium equations in 2D
cards.b: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point. They give three independent equations for a single free body in a plane.

cards.f: Reactions at a pin support
cards.b: Two force components (horizontal and vertical) and no moment. A roller gives one force perpendicular to its surface; a fixed support gives two forces and a moment.

cards.f: Newton's third law in structural analysis
cards.b: Internal forces on the two sides of a cut are equal and opposite, so a structure can be split into free bodies and each analysed separately.

cards.f: Free body diagram (FBD)
cards.b: A sketch of a body isolated from its surroundings, with every support replaced by its reactions and all loads, dimensions and a sign convention shown.

cards.f: Resultant of a UDL w over length a
cards.b: A single force wa acting at the centre of the loaded length. Use it for reactions only; for internal forces cut the beam first.

cards.f: Meaning of a negative reaction in your answer
cards.b: The real force acts in the opposite direction to the one you assumed on the FBD; the magnitude is still correct.

cards.f: Statically determinate structure
cards.b: One whose reactions and internal forces can all be found from equilibrium alone, without considering deformations.

cards.f: Degree of indeterminacy of a plane truss
cards.b: m + r − 2j (members + reaction components − 2 × joints). Zero: determinate; positive: redundant; negative: mechanism.

cards.f: Degree of indeterminacy of a rigid plane frame
cards.b: 3m + r − 3j − c, where c is the number of releases such as internal pins.

cards.f: Propped cantilever: degree of indeterminacy
cards.b: One. A fixed support (3 reactions) plus a roller (1) gives r = 4 against 3 equilibrium equations.

cards.f: Why the counting rule is not sufficient
cards.b: A structure can satisfy the count yet be unstable, e.g. all reactions parallel or concurrent, or members badly arranged. Geometry must also be checked.

cards.f: Effect of support settlement on a determinate structure
cards.b: None on the internal forces: a determinate structure can move freely to accommodate it, whereas an indeterminate one develops extra stresses.

cards.f: Hooke's law
cards.b: σ = Eε: in the linear elastic range stress is proportional to strain, with Young's modulus E as the constant.

cards.f: Axial extension of a uniform bar
cards.b: δ = FL/(EA). EA is the axial rigidity; EA/L is the axial stiffness of the bar.

cards.f: Units of stress
cards.b: N/mm², which equals MPa (1 N/mm² = 10⁶ N/m²).

cards.f: Approximate Young's modulus of structural steel
Principle of superposition
cards.b: For linear elastic, small-deflection behaviour, the effects of separate loads can be added to give the effect of the combined loads.

cards.f: Thermal stress in a fully restrained bar
cards.b: σ = EαΔT, because the free thermal strain αΔT is entirely prevented.

cards.f: Tie versus strut
cards.b: A tie carries axial tension; a strut carries axial compression (and can buckle if slender).

cards.f: Assumptions of an ideal pin-jointed truss
cards.b: Straight members, frictionless pin joints and loads applied only at joints, so every member carries axial force only.

cards.f: Method of joints
cards.b: Apply ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at each joint in turn, starting where there are at most two unknown member forces.

cards.f: Method of sections
cards.b: Cut through up to three members (not all concurrent) and take moments about the intersection of two of them to find the third directly.

cards.f: Zero-force members at an unloaded joint
cards.b: Two non-collinear members meeting at an unloaded joint carry zero force; if two of three members are collinear, the third carries zero force.

cards.f: Sign convention for truss member forces
cards.b: Tension positive (member pulls on the joint), compression negative. Assume tension; a negative answer means compression.

cards.f: Diagonals of a Pratt truss under gravity load
cards.b: In tension: the diagonals slope down towards mid-span, so the verticals are in compression and the diagonals in tension.

cards.f: dM/dx
cards.b: Equals the shear force V, so the bending moment has a maximum or minimum where V = 0.

cards.f: dV/dx
cards.b: Equals −w, minus the downward load intensity, so a UDL gives a sloping straight SFD.

cards.f: Max moment, simply supported span with UDL w
cards.b: wL²/8 at mid-span, with reactions wL/2.

cards.f: Max moment, simply supported span with central point load P
cards.b: PL/4 at mid-span.

cards.f: Point of contraflexure
cards.b: A point where the bending moment changes sign (sagging to hogging), so M = 0 there.

cards.f: Effect of a point load on the SFD
cards.b: A step (jump) in the SFD equal to the load; the BMD has a kink at that point.

cards.f: Sagging moment
cards.b: Bends the beam concave upwards, with the bottom fibre in tension; taken as positive in the usual convention.

cards.f: Engineer's bending equation
cards.b: M/I = σ/y = E/R. Assumes plane sections remain plane, linear elastic material and bending about a principal axis.

cards.f: Elastic section modulus
cards.b: Z = I/y_max, so σ_max = M/Z. For a rectangle Z = bd²/6.

cards.f: Second moment of area of a rectangle
cards.b: I = bd³/12 about its centroidal axis parallel to b.

cards.f: Parallel axis theorem
cards.b: I = I_G + Ah², where h is the distance from the part's own centroid to the axis.

cards.f: Shear stress formula
cards.b: τ = VQ/(Ib): Q is the first moment of the area beyond the level, b the width at that level.

cards.f: Maximum shear stress in a rectangular section
cards.b: 1.5 V/A at the neutral axis; the distribution is parabolic, zero at the top and bottom.

cards.f: Where is the neutral axis in elastic bending?
cards.b: Through the centroid of the cross-section.

cards.f: Differential equation of the elastic line
cards.b: EI d²v/dx² = M(x), for small deflections of a linear elastic beam.

cards.f: Cantilever tip deflection, tip load P
cards.b: PL³/(3EI).

cards.f: Simply supported mid-span deflection, UDL w
Simply supported mid-span deflection, central point load P
cards.b: PL³/(48EI).

cards.f: Boundary conditions at a fixed support
cards.b: Deflection v = 0 and slope dv/dx = 0.

cards.f: Effect of doubling the span (UDL) on deflection
cards.b: ×16, because deflection is proportional to L⁴ for a uniformly distributed load.

cards.f: Macaulay's method
cards.b: Uses singularity brackets ⟨x − a⟩ so a single bending moment expression covers a beam with several point loads.

cards.f: Unit load method for a truss
cards.b: δ = Σ FuL/(EA): F real member forces, u forces from a unit load at the point and in the direction of δ.

cards.f: Unit load method for a beam or frame
cards.b: δ = ∫Mm dx/(EI), with M from the real loads and m from the unit load, neglecting axial and shear deformation.

cards.f: Rotation by virtual work
cards.b: Apply a unit moment at the point instead of a unit force and evaluate ∫Mm dx/(EI).

cards.f: Truss deflection from temperature change
cards.b: δ = Σ u ΔL with ΔL = αΔT L for each member affected.

cards.f: Meaning of a negative result in the unit load method
cards.b: The deflection is in the opposite direction to the unit load you applied.

cards.f: Principle of virtual work
cards.b: For a body in equilibrium undergoing a compatible virtual displacement, external virtual work equals internal virtual work.

cards.f: Rigid joint
cards.b: A joint that transmits moment and keeps the angle between connected members fixed.

cards.f: Moment at a pin in a frame
cards.b: Zero (unless a concentrated moment is applied there); this gives an extra equation in a three-pinned frame.

cards.f: Tension-side convention for frame BMDs
cards.b: The bending moment is plotted on the side of each member that is in tension, so no sign is needed.

cards.f: Horizontal thrust in a symmetric three-pinned portal under UDL on the beam
cards.b: H = wL²/(8h), where L is the span and h the column height to the crown level.

cards.f: Moment at a two-member rigid joint with no applied moment
cards.b: The same value on both members either side of the joint: the BMD is continuous round the corner.

cards.f: Sway in a portal frame
cards.b: Sideways displacement of the beam level, caused by horizontal loads or by unsymmetrical geometry or loading.

cards.f: Euler critical load, pin-ended column
cards.b: P_cr = π²EI/L², using the smaller second moment of area.

cards.f: Effective length factors
cards.b: Pinned–pinned 1.0, fixed–free 2.0, fixed–pinned about 0.7, fixed–fixed 0.5 (theoretical values).

cards.f: Slenderness ratio
cards.b: λ = L_e/r, with radius of gyration r = √(I/A).

cards.f: Euler critical stress
cards.b: σ_cr = π²E/λ²; valid only when it is below the yield stress.

cards.f: Squash load
cards.b: f_y A: the load at which a stocky column yields in compression without buckling.

cards.f: Why real columns fail below the Euler load
cards.b: Initial crookedness, load eccentricity and residual stresses cause bending and yielding before ideal elastic buckling.

questions.q: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a single 30 kN point load 2 m from the left support A. What is the vertical reaction at A?
questions.why: Moments about B: R_A × 6 = 30 × 4, so R_A = 20 kN; the support nearer the load carries more. 10 kN is the reaction at B (it comes from using the 2 m distance, i.e. taking moments about A). 15 kN splits the load equally and ignores its position. 30 kN wrongly assumes the nearer support takes the whole load.

questions.q: How many independent equilibrium equations are available for a single rigid body loaded in a plane?
questions.why: In 2D there are two force equations (ΣFx, ΣFy) and one moment equation (ΣM), giving three. Two forgets the moment equation. Four double-counts by taking moments about a second point, which is not independent. Six is the number for a body in three dimensions.

questions.q: A cantilever 4 m long, fixed at A, carries a vertical load of 12 kN downwards and a horizontal load of 5 kN at its free end. Draw the free body diagram and find all the reactions at A.
markScheme: FBD showing horizontal and vertical reactions and a fixing moment at A
Vertical reaction 12 kN upwards
Horizontal reaction 5 kN opposite to the applied horizontal load

Fixing moment 12 × 4 = 48 kN·m, opposing the moment of the load: if the cantilever projects to the right of A the load turns it clockwise, so the fixing moment at A acts anticlockwise (the horizontal load acts along the axis and gives no moment)
questions.modelAnswer: Replace the fixed support at A by a horizontal force H, a vertical force V and a moment M. ΣFy = 0: V = 12 kN upwards. ΣFx = 0: H = 5 kN, acting opposite to the applied horizontal load. ΣM about A = 0: the vertical tip load has lever arm 4 m, so M = 12 × 4 = 48 kN·m, acting to oppose the rotation caused by the load. The 5 kN load acts along the beam's axis through A, so it contributes no moment.

questions.q: A pin-jointed plane truss has 10 members and 6 joints and is supported by a pin and a roller. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.why: m + r − 2j = 10 + 3 − 12 = 1, so the truss has one redundant member. 0 comes from counting the pin as providing only one reaction (r = 2) instead of two. −5 subtracts 3j, the joint term from the rigid-frame rule, instead of 2j (10 + 3 − 18). 13 counts the unknowns (m + r) but forgets to subtract the 2j joint equilibrium equations.

questions.q: A single-bay portal frame (two columns and a beam, rigid knees) has both column bases pinned. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.why: 3m + r − 3j − c = 3 × 3 + 4 − 3 × 4 − 0 = 1. 3 is the answer for fixed bases (r = 6). 0 is the answer for a three-pinned portal, which has an extra pin at the crown (c = 1). 2 comes from treating one base as fixed and the other as pinned (r = 5).

questions.q: Explain, with an example of each, the difference between statically determinate, statically indeterminate and unstable (mechanism) structures. Why can a counting rule alone not prove that a structure is stable?
markScheme: Determinate: all forces from equilibrium alone; example simply supported beam (r = 3) or triangulated truss with m + r = 2j
Indeterminate: more unknowns than equations; needs compatibility; example propped cantilever or truss with extra diagonal
Mechanism: too few restraints/members; example square truss panel with no diagonal (m + r − 2j = −1)
Counting is necessary not sufficient: e.g. three parallel rollers or concurrent reactions, or badly arranged members, can satisfy the count but still be unstable
Mentions practical consequence, e.g. indeterminate structures attract stress from settlement or temperature
questions.modelAnswer: A statically determinate structure is one in which all reactions and member forces follow from the equilibrium equations alone; a simply supported beam (pin and roller, r = 3) is an example, as is a triangulated truss for which m + r − 2j = 0. A statically indeterminate structure has more unknowns than independent equilibrium equations, so compatibility of deformations and the material law are also needed; a propped cantilever (r = 4) is one degree indeterminate, and a square truss panel with both diagonals has m + r − 2j = 6 + 3 − 8 = 1. A mechanism has too few members or restraints, for example a square panel with no diagonal (4 + 3 − 8 = −1), which racks sideways. The counting rules are necessary but not sufficient: a beam on three rollers on a flat surface has r = 3 but cannot resist horizontal load because all reactions are parallel, and a truss can have the right number of members overall while one panel is over-braced and another is a mechanism. So the geometry must always be inspected as well. In practice indeterminate structures offer redundancy but attract stresses from settlement and temperature change.

questions.q: A steel bar 2 m long with cross-sectional area 500 mm² carries an axial tension of 50 kN. Taking E = 200 GPa, what is its extension?
questions.why: δ = FL/(EA) = 50 000 × 2000/(200 000 × 500) = 1.0 mm with consistent N, mm and N/mm². 0.001 mm comes from leaving L in metres (2) while using mm elsewhere. 1000 mm comes from entering E as 200 (its value in kN/mm²) while the force is in N. 0.0005 is the strain ΔL/L, which is dimensionless, mistakenly quoted as the extension.

questions.q: Which member type carries load mainly by bending and shear rather than by axial force?
questions.why: A beam spans between supports and carries transverse loads by bending and shear. A tie carries axial tension only. A strut carries axial compression only. A cable carries tension only, changing shape to suit the load.

questions.q: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C) is fixed rigidly between two walls at 15 °C with no initial stress. Calculate the stress in the rod when its temperature rises to 45 °C, and state whether it is tensile or compressive. What assumptions have you made?
markScheme: Free thermal strain = αΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴
Fully restrained, so mechanical strain = −3.6 × 10⁻⁴
σ = Eε = 200 000 × 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ = 72 N/mm², compressive
Assumptions: walls perfectly rigid, linear elastic below yield, no buckling, uniform temperature
questions.modelAnswer: The rod would expand freely by a strain αΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × (45 − 15) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴. The rigid walls prevent any change in length, so an equal and opposite mechanical strain is imposed, giving a compressive stress σ = Eε = 200 000 × 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ = 72 N/mm². Assumptions: the walls are perfectly rigid; the steel stays linear elastic (72 N/mm² is well below typical yield stresses); the temperature is uniform along the rod; and the rod does not buckle under the compressive force.

questions.q: A triangular truss has span 4 m and its apex at mid-span 1.5 m above the supports. A 30 kN vertical load acts at the apex. What is the force in the horizontal bottom tie?
questions.why: Each support reaction is 15 kN. At a support, the rafter force is 15/sin θ = 15/0.6 = 25 kN compression, and its horizontal component, 25 × 0.8 = 20 kN, must be balanced by 20 kN tension in the tie. 15 kN is the support reaction, not a member force. 25 kN compression is the rafter force, not the tie force. 11.25 kN comes from swapping sine and cosine: taking the rafter force as 15/0.8 = 18.75 kN and its horizontal component as 18.75 × 0.6.

questions.q: At an unloaded joint, three members meet; two of them are collinear. What can you conclude?
options: The two collinear members are zero-force
questions.why: Resolving perpendicular to the collinear pair, only the third member has a component, so its force must be zero; the collinear members carry equal forces. Saying all three are zero confuses this with the two-member rule. Saying the collinear pair is zero reverses the rule. No reactions are needed, because the joint is unloaded and equilibrium at the joint alone decides it.

questions.q: A Pratt truss has four 3 m panels and a height of 4 m. It is simply supported at its ends and carries 20 kN at each of the three interior bottom-chord joints. Use the method of sections to find the forces in the top chord, bottom chord and diagonal of the second panel from the left (the diagonal slopes down towards mid-span). State tension or compression.
markScheme: Reactions 30 kN each by symmetry
Top chord: moments about bottom joint at 6 m: (30 × 6 − 20 × 3)/4 = 30 kN compression
Bottom chord: moments about top joint at 3 m: 30 × 3/4 = 22.5 kN tension
Diagonal: panel shear 10 kN, length 5 m, force 10 × 5/4 = 12.5 kN tension
Check: horizontal components sum to zero (−30 + 22.5 + 7.5 = 0)
questions.modelAnswer: Total load 60 kN, so each reaction is 30 kN. Cut through the second panel (between x = 3 m and x = 6 m) and take the left-hand part. Top chord: take moments about the bottom joint at x = 6 m, through which the bottom chord and diagonal pass: 30 × 6 − 20 × 3 = 120 kN·m, so the force is 120/4 = 30 kN, compression (the top chord pushes). Bottom chord: take moments about the top joint at x = 3 m: 30 × 3 = 90 kN·m, so the force is 90/4 = 22.5 kN tension. Diagonal: the net vertical force on the left part is 30 − 20 = 10 kN upwards, which only the diagonal can balance; the diagonal is 5 m long with a vertical projection of 4 m, so its force is 10 × 5/4 = 12.5 kN, tension. Check horizontally: −30 + 22.5 + 12.5 × 3/5 = 0.

questions.q: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over its whole length. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.why: M_max = wL²/8 = 10 × 64/8 = 80 kN·m at mid-span. 40 kN·m confuses the moment with the reaction (wL/2 = 40 kN). 160 kN·m applies the central point-load result PL/4 with the whole load (P = wL = 80 kN) concentrated at mid-span. 320 kN·m is wL²/2, the support moment of a cantilever of the same length.

questions.q: On a beam segment carrying a uniformly distributed load, what shapes are the shear force and bending moment diagrams?
options: SFD straight sloping line, BMD parabola
SFD horizontal, BMD straight sloping line
questions.why: Since dV/dx = −w is constant, V is linear (a sloping straight line), and since dM/dx = V is linear, M is quadratic (a parabola). Horizontal SFD with a straight BMD describes an unloaded segment. Both straight is wrong because M must curve when V varies. Parabolic SFD with cubic BMD describes a linearly varying (triangular) load.

questions.q: A beam is pinned at A (x = 0), on a roller at B (x = 6 m) and overhangs to a free end C (x = 8 m). It carries a UDL of 10 kN/m over its full length. Find the reactions, the maximum sagging moment and its position, the moment at B, and the position of the point of contraflexure. Sketch the BMD.
markScheme: V = 26.7 − 10x = 0 at x = 2.67 m; M_max = 35.6 kN·m sagging
M_B = −10 × 2²/2 = −20 kN·m (hogging)
Contraflexure where 26.7x − 5x² = 0: x = 5.33 m
Sketch: parabola from 0 at A to +35.6 at 2.67 m, through zero at 5.33 m, −20 at B, back to 0 at C
questions.modelAnswer: Total load 80 kN at x = 4 m. Moments about A: R_B × 6 = 80 × 4, so R_B = 53.3 kN; R_A = 80 − 53.3 = 26.7 kN. In span AB, V(x) = 26.7 − 10x, zero at x = 2.67 m, where M = 26.7 × 2.67 − 5 × 2.67² = 35.6 kN·m sagging. At B, taking the overhang: M_B = −10 × 2 × 1 = −20 kN·m (hogging). In AB, M(x) = 26.7x − 5x², which is zero at x = 0 and x = 2 × 26.7/10 = 5.33 m, the point of contraflexure. The BMD is a parabola rising to 35.6 kN·m, crossing zero at 5.33 m, reaching −20 kN·m over B and returning to zero at the free end C.

questions.q: A rectangular timber beam 100 mm wide and 300 mm deep carries a bending moment of 20 kN·m. What is the maximum bending stress?
questions.why: Z = bd²/6 = 100 × 300²/6 = 1.5 × 10⁶ mm³, so σ = 20 × 10⁶/1.5 × 10⁶ = 13.3 N/mm². 26.7 N/mm² uses y = d (300 mm) instead of y = d/2 in σ = My/I. 40 N/mm² swaps b and d, as if the beam were laid on its side. 0.089 N/mm² divides M by I (2.25 × 10⁸ mm⁴) as though I were the section modulus, forgetting y.

questions.q: Where is the shear stress greatest in a rectangular beam section carrying a vertical shear force?
options: At a quarter of the depth from the top
At the top and bottom fibres
questions.why: τ = VQ/(Ib) is largest where Q, the first moment of the area beyond the level, is greatest, which is at the neutral axis; there τ = 1.5V/A. At the top and bottom fibres Q = 0, so τ = 0; that is where bending stress, not shear stress, peaks. Uniform shear stress V/A is only an average. A quarter depth is an arbitrary level where τ is three quarters of the maximum.

questions.q: A T-section has a flange 200 mm × 20 mm and a web 20 mm × 180 mm (total depth 200 mm). Find the position of the neutral axis and the second moment of area about it. Hence find the maximum tensile and compressive stresses under a sagging moment of 10 kN·m.
markScheme: Top (compression): σ = 10 × 10⁶ × 57.4/28.8 × 10⁶ ≈ 19.9 N/mm²
Bottom (tension): σ = 10 × 10⁶ × 142.6/28.8 × 10⁶ ≈ 49.5 N/mm²
States sagging puts top in compression and bottom in tension
questions.modelAnswer: Areas: flange 4000 mm² with centroid 10 mm below the top; web 3600 mm² with centroid 20 + 90 = 110 mm below the top. Neutral axis: ȳ = (4000 × 10 + 3600 × 110)/7600 = 57.4 mm below the top (142.6 mm above the bottom). Parallel axis theorem: I = 200 × 20³/12 + 4000 × (57.4 − 10)² + 20 × 180³/12 + 3600 × (110 − 57.4)² ≈ 0.13 × 10⁶ + 8.98 × 10⁶ + 9.72 × 10⁶ + 9.97 × 10⁶ ≈ 28.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Under a sagging moment the top is in compression and the bottom in tension. Top: σ = 10 × 10⁶ × 57.4/28.8 × 10⁶ ≈ 19.9 N/mm² compression. Bottom: σ = 10 × 10⁶ × 142.6/28.8 × 10⁶ ≈ 49.5 N/mm² tension. The bottom stress is larger because the bottom fibre is further from the neutral axis.

questions.q: A simply supported beam carries a uniformly distributed load. If the span is doubled with the same load per metre and the same section, the mid-span deflection becomes:
questions.why: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI), so doubling L multiplies δ by 2⁴ = 16. 8 times uses the L³ dependence of a point-load formula. 4 times uses the L² dependence of the bending moment wL²/8. 2 times assumes deflection is simply proportional to span.

questions.q: A steel cantilever of length 2 m carries a 5 kN point load at its tip. EI = 4000 kN·m². What is the tip deflection?
questions.why: δ = PL³/(3EI) = 5 × 8/(3 × 4000) = 0.00333 m = 3.3 mm. 10 mm omits the factor 3, using PL³/EI. 5.0 mm uses PL³/(2EI), confusing the deflection with the tip-slope coefficient PL²/(2EI). 1.25 mm uses the cantilever UDL coefficient, PL³/(8EI), treating the point load as if it were spread along the beam.

questions.q: Using double integration, derive the tip deflection of a cantilever of length L, fixed at x = 0, carrying a uniformly distributed load w over its whole length. State your sign convention and boundary conditions.
markScheme: Convention: v upwards, sagging M positive; EI v″ = M
M(x) = −w(L − x)²/2
EI v′ = w(L − x)³/6 + C₁; v′(0) = 0 gives C₁ = −wL³/6
EI v = −w(L − x)⁴/24 − wL³x/6 + C₂; v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = wL⁴/24
At x = L: EI v = −wL⁴/6 + wL⁴/24 = −wL⁴/8, so δ = wL⁴/(8EI) downwards
questions.modelAnswer: Take v positive upwards and sagging moments positive, so EI v″ = M. At a section x from the support, the load on the free part is w(L − x) acting at (L − x)/2, giving a hogging moment M(x) = −w(L − x)²/2. Integrating: EI v′ = w(L − x)³/6 + C₁ (check: differentiating gives −w(L − x)²/2). At the fixed end v′(0) = 0, so C₁ = −wL³/6. Integrating again: EI v = −w(L − x)⁴/24 − wL³x/6 + C₂. At the fixed end v(0) = 0: −wL⁴/24 + C₂ = 0, so C₂ = wL⁴/24. At the tip x = L: EI v = 0 − wL⁴/6 + wL⁴/24 = −wL⁴/8. The tip deflection is therefore wL⁴/(8EI) downwards.

questions.q: In the unit load method for a pin-jointed truss, δ = Σ FuL/(EA). What does u represent?
options: The extension of each member under the real loads
The member force caused by a unit load applied at the point, in the direction of the deflection required
A unit length of each member
The member force caused by the real loads
questions.why: u is the virtual member force from a unit load placed where, and in the direction in which, the deflection is wanted. The member force from the real loads is F, not u. The real extension is FL/(EA), the deformation that u multiplies. 'Unit length' confuses the unit load with a unit of length.

questions.q: For the triangular truss (span 4 m, rise 1.5 m, 30 kN at apex) the real forces are −25 kN in each 2.5 m rafter and +20 kN in the 4 m tie. All members have EA = 200 000 kN. What is the vertical deflection of the apex?
questions.why: With a unit load at the apex, u = −0.833 in each rafter and +0.667 in the tie. Σ FuL = 2 × (−25)(−0.833)(2.5) + 20 × 0.667 × 4 = 104.2 + 53.3 = 157.5 kN·m, so δ = 157.5/200 000 m = 0.79 mm. 0.53 mm includes only one rafter (52.1 + 53.3 = 105.4 kN·m). 0.27 mm keeps only the tie term (53.3 kN·m). 23.6 mm uses Σ F²L/(EA) = 4725/200 000 m, i.e. the real force in place of u, which is not a deflection at all.

questions.q: Use virtual work to find the vertical deflection of the tip of a cantilever of length L carrying a downward point load P at the tip. Then explain how the method would change to find the rotation at the tip.
markScheme: Apply a unit vertical load at the tip; with x from the tip, M = Px and m = x (same sign convention)
δ = ∫₀ᴸ Mm dx/(EI) = ∫₀ᴸ Px² dx/(EI)
δ = PL³/(3EI) downwards
For rotation, apply a unit moment at the tip: m = 1 everywhere
θ = ∫₀ᴸ Px dx/(EI) = PL²/(2EI)
questions.modelAnswer: Apply a virtual unit load at the tip in the direction of the deflection wanted (downwards). Measuring x from the tip, the real moment is M = Px and the virtual moment is m = 1 × x, both hogging, so they have the same sign. Then δ = ∫₀ᴸ Mm dx/(EI) = ∫₀ᴸ Px² dx/(EI) = PL³/(3EI), downwards (positive, so in the direction of the unit load). For the tip rotation, apply a unit moment at the tip instead: the virtual moment is m = 1 along the whole length, so θ = ∫₀ᴸ Px dx/(EI) = PL²/(2EI). Both match the standard double integration results.

questions.q: A three-pinned portal frame has pinned bases, columns 5 m high, a 10 m horizontal beam with a pin at mid-span, and a UDL of 10 kN/m on the beam. What is the horizontal reaction at each base?
questions.why: Vertical reactions are wL/2 = 50 kN. Moments about the crown pin for the left half: 50 × 5 − H × 5 − 10 × 5 × 2.5 = 0, so H = 25 kN (= wL²/(8h)). 50 kN is the vertical reaction. 125 kN is the knee moment Hh in kN·m, not a force. 12.5 kN wrongly shares the thrust between the two bases; in fact each base carries the full 25 kN, equal and opposite to the other.

questions.q: At a rigid joint where only two members meet and no external moment is applied, how do the bending moments in the two members just either side of the joint compare?
options: They depend on the member lengths and are generally different
They are equal, so the BMD is continuous round the corner
They are equal and opposite, so the BMD changes sides
questions.why: Moment equilibrium of the small joint requires the two end moments to balance, so the moment carries round the corner with the same value and on the same (inside or outside) face. They are zero only at a pin or free end, not at a rigid joint. 'Changes sides' misreads equal-and-opposite end actions as a change of tension face. Member lengths affect the value but not the equality at a two-member joint.

questions.q: An L-shaped frame has a vertical column AB, 3 m high, fixed at the base A, and a horizontal arm BC, 2 m long, rigidly connected at B. A 10 kN downward load acts at C. Find the reactions at A and sketch the bending moment, shear and axial force diagrams, stating values at key points.
markScheme: Reactions at A: vertical 10 kN upwards, no horizontal reaction, fixing moment 20 kN·m
Arm BC: shear 10 kN constant; M zero at C rising linearly to 20 kN·m at B, tension on the top face
Column AB: constant M = 20 kN·m from B to A, tension on the outer face (the side away from the arm); no shear
Column axial force 10 kN compression; arm axial force zero
Moment of 20 kN·m continuous round the outside of the rigid joint B
questions.modelAnswer: Overall equilibrium: the vertical reaction at A is 10 kN upwards; there are no horizontal loads, so the horizontal reaction is zero; moments about A give a fixing moment of 10 × 2 = 20 kN·m. Arm BC acts as a cantilever from B: shear 10 kN throughout, bending moment zero at C rising linearly to 20 kN·m at B, with tension on the top face. At the rigid joint B the 20 kN·m moment carries round the outside of the corner: the top face of the arm continues as the outer face of the column (the side away from the arm). In column AB the moment is constant at 20 kN·m from B down to A, with tension on that outer face; the column carries no shear (there is no horizontal load) and 10 kN axial compression. The arm carries no axial force.

questions.q: A slender column is pinned at both ends. If the end conditions are changed to fixed at both ends (same length and section), the theoretical Euler critical load:
questions.why: Fixed–fixed gives an effective length of 0.5L, and P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², so P_cr rises by a factor of 1/0.5² = 4. Doubling treats P_cr as inversely proportional to L_e rather than L_e². Dividing by 4 is the effect of changing to fixed–free (L_e = 2L). Halving reverses the effect of fixity and uses the wrong power.

questions.q: A 3 m pin-ended solid steel bar of diameter 50 mm (E = 200 GPa) has an Euler load of about 67 kN. A bar of the same length and material with diameter 100 mm would have an Euler load of about:
questions.why: I = πd⁴/64, so doubling d multiplies I and hence P_cr by 2⁴ = 16: 67.3 × 16 ≈ 1077 kN. 135 kN assumes P_cr ∝ d. 269 kN assumes P_cr ∝ d², i.e. proportional to area rather than second moment of area. 538 kN assumes P_cr ∝ d³, mixing up I with the section modulus.

questions.q: A 3 m long solid circular steel strut of diameter 50 mm is pinned at both ends. E = 200 GPa and f_y = 275 N/mm². Calculate the Euler critical load, the squash load and the slenderness ratio, and state which failure mode governs and why Euler theory is valid here.
markScheme: Squash load = 275 × 1963 ≈ 540 kN
Buckling governs; σ_cr = π²E/λ² ≈ 34 N/mm² < f_y, so elastic (Euler) buckling applies
questions.modelAnswer: Section properties: I = πd⁴/64 = π × 50⁴/64 = 3.07 × 10⁵ mm⁴ and A = πd²/4 = 1963 mm². Euler load (pin-ended, L_e = L): P_cr = π²EI/L² = π² × 200 000 × 3.07 × 10⁵/3000² = 67.3 × 10³ N = 67.3 kN. Squash load: f_y A = 275 × 1963 = 540 kN. Radius of gyration r = √(I/A) = d/4 = 12.5 mm, so λ = 3000/12.5 = 240. The strut buckles at about 67 kN, far below the squash load, so buckling governs. Euler theory is valid because the critical stress σ_cr = π²E/λ² = 34 N/mm² is well below the yield stress, so the strut is still elastic when it buckles. In reality, imperfections would reduce the failure load somewhat below 67 kN.

questions.q:
An L-shaped frame ABC has a vertical column AB of height h = 3 m, fixed at A, and a horizontal arm BC of length a = 2 m rigidly connected at B. A vertical load P = 10 kN acts downwards at C. EI = 20 000 kN·m² for both members; axial and shear deformations may be neglected.
(a) Determine the reactions at A. [3]
(b) Draw the bending moment diagram for the frame on the tension side, giving key values. [4]
(c) Using the principle of virtual work, determine the vertical deflection at C. [7]
(d) Using virtual work, determine the magnitude and direction of the horizontal deflection at C. [6]
markScheme: (a) V_A = 10 kN upwards, H_A = 0, M_A = 20 kN·m
(b) Arm: 0 at C rising to 20 kN·m at B, tension on top; column: constant 20 kN·m, tension on the outer face, continuous round the outside of joint B
(c) Unit vertical load at C: m = x in arm, m = 2 in column; same tension faces as M
(d) Unit horizontal load at C: m = 0 in arm (acts along its axis), m = y in column measured down from B
(d) Correct direction from the sign of the product: C moves horizontally towards the side the arm projects to (the column top tilts towards the load)
Consistent units (kN, m, kN·m²) and clearly stated sign convention
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Vertical equilibrium gives V_A = 10 kN upwards. There are no horizontal loads, so H_A = 0. Moments about A: the load has a horizontal lever arm of 2 m, so M_A = 10 × 2 = 20 kN·m.

(b) In the arm, measuring x from C, M = 10x, rising from 0 at C to 20 kN·m at B, with tension on the top face. At the rigid joint B the moment carries round the outside of the corner, so the column has a constant moment of 20 kN·m from B to A, with tension on its outer face (the side away from the arm).

(c) Apply a unit downward load at C. Its moments are m = x in the arm and m = 2 in the column, with the same tension faces as the real moments, so the products are positive:
δ_v = (1/EI)[∫₀² (10x)(x) dx + ∫₀³ (20)(2) dy] = (1/EI)[26.7 + 120] = 146.7/20 000 = 0.00733 m = 7.33 mm downwards.
Most of this comes from the column, whose rotation swings the whole arm down.

(d) Apply a unit horizontal load at C acting in the direction from B towards C (away from the column). It acts along the arm's axis, so m = 0 in the arm. In the column, measuring y down from B, its moment is 1 × y, and, like the real load, it bends the column with tension on the outer face (both turn the column top clockwise if the arm points to the right), so M and m have the same sense. The product is therefore positive:
δ_h = (1/EI) ∫₀³ (20)(y) dy = (20 × 3²/2)/20 000 = 90/20 000 = 0.0045 m = 4.5 mm,
in the direction of the unit load, i.e. C moves horizontally in the direction from B towards C. Physically, the constant moment curves the column so that its top rotates and translates towards the side on which the load hangs. In general δ_h = Pah²/(2EI).

Check on (d): a column under constant moment M₀ deflects at its top by M₀h²/(2EI) = 20 × 9/(2 × 20 000) = 4.5 mm, and B and C share this horizontal movement because the arm is axially rigid.

questions.q:
A beam ABC is simply supported at A and B, 8 m apart, and has an overhang BC of 2 m. It carries a point load of 40 kN at mid-span of AB and a UDL of 15 kN/m on the overhang BC only.
(a) Calculate the support reactions. [4]
(b) Draw the shear force and bending moment diagrams, stating your sign convention and giving all key values. [8]
(c) Find the position of any point of contraflexure. [3]
(d) The beam is a rectangular timber section 150 mm wide. Choose the minimum depth (to the nearest 10 mm) if the bending stress must not exceed 12 N/mm². [5]
markScheme: (b) Convention stated; SFD: +16.25 from A to load, −23.75 from load to B, jump to +30 at B, linear to 0 at C
(b) BMD: 0 at A, +65 kN·m under load, −30 kN·m at B, 0 at C (parabolic on overhang)
(c) Between load and B: M = 65 − 23.75s = 0 at s = 2.74 m beyond the load, i.e. x ≈ 6.74 m from A
(d) Design moment 65 kN·m (largest magnitude); Z required = 65 × 10⁶/12 = 5.42 × 10⁶ mm³
Units and working clear throughout
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Loads: 40 kN at x = 4 m and 15 × 2 = 30 kN acting at x = 9 m (centre of the overhang). Moments about A: 8R_B = 40 × 4 + 30 × 9 = 160 + 270 = 430, so R_B = 53.75 kN. Vertical equilibrium: R_A = 70 − 53.75 = 16.25 kN.

(b) Convention: shear positive when the resultant of forces to the left is upwards; sagging moment positive.
SFD: +16.25 kN from A to x = 4 m; drops by 40 to −23.75 kN from x = 4 m to B; jumps up by 53.75 to +30 kN just right of B; falls linearly at 15 kN/m to 0 at C.
BMD: 0 at A; at x = 4 m, M = 16.25 × 4 = +65 kN·m (sagging); at B, M = 65 − 23.75 × 4 = −30 kN·m (hogging), which agrees with the overhang: −15 × 2²/2 = −30 kN·m; on the overhang M is parabolic from −30 kN·m to 0 at C. Between A and B the BMD is straight-line segments.

(c) Between the load and B, M = 65 − 23.75s, where s is the distance beyond the load. M = 0 at s = 65/23.75 = 2.74 m, so the point of contraflexure is about 6.74 m from A.

(d) The largest moment magnitude is 65 kN·m (sagging). Required section modulus Z = M/σ = 65 × 10⁶/12 = 5.42 × 10⁶ mm³. For a rectangle Z = bd²/6, so d = √(6Z/b) = √(6 × 5.42 × 10⁶/150) = 466 mm. Choose d = 470 mm (rounding up), giving Z = 150 × 470²/6 = 5.52 × 10⁶ mm³ and σ = 11.8 N/mm² ≤ 12 N/mm². A full design would also check shear (τ_max = 1.5V/A with V = 30 kN gives about 0.64 N/mm²) and deflection.
